parts.title: Joining a sports centre
parts.intro: You will hear a man talking to a receptionist at a community sports centre.

script.t: Good afternoon, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help?
Hi. I’ve just moved to the area and I’m thinking of joining the centre. Could you tell me a bit about the membership options?
Of course. We have three types of membership. There’s Basic, which gives you the gym and the pool, Active, which adds all the exercise classes, and Family, for two adults and up to three children.
It’s just me, so probably Basic or Active. What do they cost?
Basic is £32 a month, and Active is £45.
script.say: Basic is thirty-two pounds a month, and Active is forty-five.

script.t: Hmm. Is there a joining fee?
Normally there’s a joining fee of £20, but this month we’re not charging it for new members.
script.say: Normally there’s a joining fee of twenty pounds, but this month we’re not charging it for new members.

script.t: Oh, good timing. I think I’ll go for Active, then. I used to do a lot of classes where I lived before.
Lovely. I can start the form for you now if you like. Can I take your full name?
Yes, it’s Peter Gaskell. That’s G, A, S, K, E, double L.
script.say: Yes, it’s Peter Gaskell. That’s G, A, S, K, E, double L.

script.t: And your address?
It’s Flat 3, 27 Kingsley Road.
script.say: It’s Flat three, twenty-seven Kingsley Road.

script.t: Kingsley, like the name?
Exactly. K, I, N, G, S, L, E, Y. Kingsley.
script.say: Exactly. K, I, N, G, S, L, E, Y. Kingsley.

script.t: And the postcode?
It’s RM4 8TJ.
script.say: It’s R, M, four, eight, T, J.

script.t: Thank you. Date of birth?
The 9th of March, 1994.
script.say: The ninth of March, nineteen ninety-four.

script.t: And how did you hear about us? We like to keep track.
I saw a leaflet in the library, actually, although a neighbour had mentioned you as well.
I’ll put the leaflet, then. Now, do you have any medical conditions we should know about? Anything that might affect your exercise?
Not really. I had a knee injury a couple of years ago from playing football, but it’s completely fine now.
OK, I’ll make a note of the knee anyway, so the instructors are aware.
Can I ask about the classes? What’s the most popular?
Probably the cycling class. It’s on Tuesday and Thursday evenings at seven, and it fills up very quickly, so you have to book online at least two days before.
Right. And is there anything for beginners? I haven’t swum for years.
There’s an adult swimming class on Saturday mornings. It’s run by Martin, who’s very patient. The class starts at 8.30.
script.say: There’s an adult swimming class on Saturday mornings. It’s run by Martin, who’s very patient. The class starts at eight thirty.

script.t: That’s early!
It is, but the pool is much quieter then. Oh, and with Active membership you also get a free session with a personal trainer, who’ll design a programme for you.
That sounds useful. How do I book that?
Just ask at reception when you come in for your induction. Everyone has to do an induction before using the gym. It takes about forty minutes.
Fine. What should I bring on the first day?
Your bank details, so we can set up the monthly payment, and a photo for your membership card. We don’t take the photo here, I’m afraid, so please bring one with you.
Do I need a padlock for the lockers?
No, the lockers use a coin, which you get back. And towels can be hired for a pound, but most people bring their own.
script.say: No, the lockers use a coin, which you get back. And towels can be hired for a pound, but most people bring their own.

script.t: Great. And is there parking?
There is, but it’s limited in the evenings. If you can, it’s better to come by bike. We’ve got plenty of covered racks at the side of the building.
That’s perfect. I’ll come in tomorrow, then. Thanks very much.

parts.title: The Harwick Summer Arts Festival
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter talking about a local summer arts festival.

script.t: And now for some good news for anyone looking for things to do this summer. The Harwick Arts Festival is back, and this year it’s bigger than ever. I’ve been looking through the programme, and I’d like to tell you about some of the highlights.
First, the dates. The festival usually runs for a fortnight in July, but this year the organisers have decided to extend it to three weeks, starting on the first Saturday of the month.

One reason for the extension is that the festival has a new main venue. In the past, most events took place in the old town hall, which only holds a few hundred people. This year the big concerts will be in the newly restored railway warehouse by the river.

Now, I know a lot of listeners have complained about ticket prices in previous years. Well, the organisers have listened. Prices for the main concerts haven’t changed, but every afternoon event is now free, and that includes the children’s theatre.

Something else that’s new is the way you buy tickets. You can still get them from the box office, but the organisers are encouraging people to use the festival app, because it shows which events still have seats and sends you a reminder on the day.

If you’re planning to drive, be warned: parking in the town centre will be very limited. The festival has arranged a park-and-ride service from the football stadium, with buses every fifteen minutes until midnight.
script.say: If you’re planning to drive, be warned: parking in the town centre will be very limited. The festival has arranged a park-and-ride service from the football stadium, with buses every fifteen minutes until midnight.

script.t: OK, so what should you see? Here are my personal recommendations.

On the opening weekend there’s a performance by the Northgate Youth Orchestra. They’re all teenagers, but honestly, you’d never know it. Amazingly, this is the first time they’ve ever played at the festival, and they’ll be performing some well-known film music.

For something completely different, there’s the street theatre in the market square. The performers walk on stilts and wear enormous masks. It’s best for families, and it happens every afternoon, so there’s no need to plan ahead.

If you prefer something quieter, go to the photography exhibition in the library. It’s called “Our River”, and it’s made up entirely of photographs taken by local residents over the past year. It’s a lovely way to see your own town through other people’s eyes.

Then there’s the poetry evening at the Blue Door café. This one is aimed at young writers. Anyone between sixteen and twenty-five can sign up to read one of their own poems on stage, and there’s a prize for the best one.

And finally, if you only see one thing, make it the closing night. There’s a big outdoor concert by the river with a firework display at the end. It’s the only event this year that’s sold out already, so if you haven’t got a ticket, you can still watch the fireworks from the bridge.
Full details are on the festival website. Now, let’s take a look at the weather.

parts.title: Planning a survey on student travel
parts.intro: You will hear two students, Aisha and Ben, planning a survey about how students travel to university.

script.t: OK, Ben, we need to get this survey planned today. Dr Hale wants a draft of our questions by Friday.
Right. So we agreed the topic is how students travel to campus and whether they’d change.
Yes. I was reading some of the previous studies last night, and there were a couple of things that stood out for me.
Go on.

Well, firstly, cost seems to matter far more than time. Students will accept a much longer journey if it saves them money. And secondly, most studies only looked at students living in university housing, which is a bit odd, because the majority live in private rented flats.
That’s a good point. So we should make sure we include both groups.
Definitely. What did you find?

I noticed that hardly anyone asked about safety, especially for students cycling or walking home late. I think that could be really important. Oh, and weather. Lots of people say they’d cycle if it didn’t rain so much.
Hmm, but we can’t do much about the weather. I’d rather focus on things the university could actually change. So safety, yes, weather, probably not.
Fair enough.
So, how shall we go about it? I think the first step is to write a short list of questions and try them out on a few friends, to see if anything’s confusing.
A pilot, yes. Then we revise the questions based on what they say.
And then we need permission. We can’t just send emails to all the students.
No, we have to get approval from the ethics committee. Dr Hale said it takes about two weeks, so we should apply as soon as the questions are ready.
OK. Once we’ve got approval, how do we reach people? I don’t think emails work. Everyone ignores them.
I agree. What about putting a QR code on posters in the library and the canteens? People can scan it and do the survey on their phones in a couple of minutes.
That’s much better. And maybe we could offer a small reward to encourage people, like entry into a prize draw.
Good idea. Then, after about three weeks, we close the survey and start the analysis.
Which will be the hard part. I’d like to compare the answers of students who live on campus with those who don’t.
And finally we present the results to the transport office. They said they’d be interested.
Great. Let’s start on the questions now, then.

parts.title: Animal camouflage
parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture about camouflage in the animal world.

script.t: Good morning. In today’s lecture we’re going to look at camouflage: the different ways in which animals avoid being seen. Camouflage is used both by animals that are hunted, so that predators don’t find them, and by predators themselves, so that they can get close to their prey without being noticed.

The simplest form of camouflage is called background matching. Here, the animal’s colour and pattern resemble its surroundings. Think of the sandy colour of many desert animals, such as the fennec fox. Background matching works well, but it has a major limitation: it only works in one type of environment. If the animal moves somewhere different, it becomes very easy to see.

Some animals solve this problem by changing colour with the seasons. The Arctic hare, for example, has a brown coat in summer and a white coat in winter. However, scientists have recently become concerned about these animals. Because of climate change, snow is arriving later and melting earlier, so for several weeks each year the hares are white against brown ground.

A second type of camouflage is known as disruptive colouration. Animals with this kind of camouflage have bold patches or stripes that break up their outline. The point is not to match the background, but to stop a predator recognising the shape of the animal. Many fish on coral reefs use this strategy.

There is a lot of debate about zebra stripes. For many years people assumed they were disruptive camouflage, but the most widely accepted explanation today is quite different: the stripes seem to discourage biting flies from landing.

A third strategy is countershading. Many animals, from sharks to deer, are darker on their back and lighter on their belly. This seems odd at first, but it makes sense when you consider light. Sunlight comes from above, so normally the top of an animal is bright and its underside is in shadow. Countershading cancels out this effect, which makes the animal look flat and much harder to notice.

Then there is masquerade, which is slightly different. Here, the animal can be seen perfectly well, but it looks like something that isn’t worth eating. Some caterpillars, for instance, look exactly like twigs, and certain spiders resemble bird droppings. A predator may look straight at them and simply not be interested.

Finally, some of the most impressive examples of camouflage are found in the sea. The cuttlefish can change its colour in less than a second. It does this using special cells in its skin, which contain different pigments and can be expanded or contracted by tiny muscles. Remarkably, cuttlefish appear to be colour-blind, so researchers are still trying to understand how they match colours so precisely.

Understanding camouflage isn’t just of interest to biologists. Designers have borrowed many of these ideas, most obviously for military uniforms, but also for buildings such as mobile phone masts, which are sometimes disguised as trees to make them less ugly.
